detail.overview:
CoLearn Lab is a Southeast Asia–based research and product organization working to develop critical thinkers and problem solvers at scale, built on insights from more than 5 million K-12 students, 60,000 parents, and 100 full-time teachers. In the CoLearn app, students in grades 4–12 practise by photographing their handwritten working, which is then evaluated by AI.

What a teacher actually needs is different. When a student writes a wrong answer, the useful information is *why*: did they add the numerators and denominators of two fractions, treat multiplication of matrices as commutative, stop at an intermediate quantity, or misread the word problem and pick the wrong operation? Each of those calls for a different intervention. Naming the misconception turns a red cross into a teaching moment — and at CoLearn's scale, into an automatic one.

That second task is far from solved. On a benchmark of 400 student workings annotated with our misconception taxonomy, the best off-the-shelf model identified the misconceptions correctly 73% of the time, and open-weight models managed 45–59%. Fine-tuning open-weight models on about 3,400 annotated workings lifted them to 63–66%: a real gain, but still short of what a teacher needs. A model that misreads a quarter of student reasoning cannot be put in front of a class.

This competition asks you to close that gap. You will receive 1,500 labelled student workings for training — the photo, the question, the answer key, our line-by-line transcription of the handwriting, and the misconception labels — and will predict the root misconception for 3,498 test workings from the photo, question and key alone. The workings are in Indonesian and English language and the handwriting is real: crossed-out lines, faint pencil, phone-camera skew.

A further 50,000 student workings are provided without labels, for teams that want to use semi-supervised methods such as pseudo-labelling or pre-training a handwriting reader.

Two things make this different from earlier misconception competitions. First, the input is an image of free-form handwritten working, not a multiple-choice distractor — the model has to find the error before it can name it. Second, a third of the workings are correct, and saying so is part of the task: a model that raises false alarms on correct work is as unusable as one that misses errors.

Why take part

- A multimodal problem with a clean, teacher-defined label space and hidden test labels.
- A realistic size: the training set fits in a notebook, the taxonomy fits in a prompt, and the whole competition runs on Kaggle's free GPU quota.
- Winning solutions are published under an open licence, so the outcome is a public, reproducible baseline for handwritten-work diagnosis in a low-resource language.

Timeline

- October 6, 2026 — Start Date.
- November 17, 2026 — Final Submission Deadline.

All deadlines are at 11:59 PM UTC on the corresponding day unless otherwise noted.…
detail.evaluation:
Submissions are evaluated on Mean Average Precision at 3 (MAP@3):

$$ \text{MAP@3} = \frac{1}{U} \sum_{u=1}^{U} \sum_{k=1}^{\min(n,3)} P(k) \times rel(k) $$

where *U* is the number of test rows, *n* is the number of predictions you submitted for that row, *P(k)* is the precision at cut-off *k*, and *rel(k)* is 1 if the code at rank *k* is the correct one and 0 otherwise.

There is exactly one correct label per row, so the score for a row is simply 1 if your first prediction is right, 1/2 if your second is, 1/3 if your third is, and 0 otherwise. The leaderboard score is the mean over rows.

Once a correct label has been scored for a row, repeats of it are skipped, so the three submissions below all score 1.0 for a row whose correct label is ALG-06:

 ALG-06 CAL-01 ANS-01
 ALG-06 ALG-06 ALG-06
 ALG-06 CAL-01 ALG-06

The label being predicted

root_code is one of the 75 taxonomy codes, or NONE. It is the misconception the rest of the working follows from — not necessarily the first error written on the page. A root is always a major misconception (one that changes the reasoning or the result).

NONE means the working contains no major misconception: it is fully correct, or carries only minor slips such as imprecise notation that do not change the result. NONE is a legitimate prediction and about a third of test rows have it.

Note that the taxonomy covers conceptual misconceptions and also procedural and careless errors (for example CAL-01, a simple arithmetic or copying slip): the root is whichever of these the rest of the working follows from, so it can be a slip as well as a wrong idea.

Why this metric

- Ranking matters in the product: a teacher reads the first suggestion, not a list.…
detail.data_or_tools:
Each row of the dataset is one trace: a single student's handwritten attempt at a single practice question, photographed with a phone. Students are in Indonesian grades 4–12 (ages roughly 9–18). The questions and the handwriting are in Bahasa Indonesia; question texts contain LaTeX for mathematical notation. The 499 questions span 61 curriculum topics: whole-number and integer operations, fractions and decimals, LCM/GCF, powers and surds, algebra, functions, measurement, geometry, statistics and probability.

What you are predicting: root_code, the taxonomy code of the root misconception in the working, or NONE if the working has no major misconception.

Files

* train.csv - 1,500 labelled rows
* test.csv - 3,498 rows without labels. The leaderboard is split 1,000 public / 2,498 private; you cannot tell which rows are which.
* sample_submission.csv - a sample submission in the correct format, with NONE for every row
* taxonomy_v1.csv - the 75 misconception codes that occur in this dataset, with name, description, nature (conceptual / procedural / careless / meta), default severity, typical grade band and section
* unlabelled.csv - 50,000 additional student workings without labels,

a. The maximum Team size is five (5).

b. Team mergers are allowed and can be performed by the Team leader. In order to merge, the combined Team must have a total Submission count less than or equal to the maximum allowed as of the Team Merger Deadline. The maximum allowed is the number of Submissions per day multiplied by the number of days the competition has been running.
